source.title: From Detection to Refusal: Safer LLMs via Circuit-Guided Weight Scaling
source.authors: Kuan-Lin Chu; Chung-En Sun; T. Weng

record.tranche_reason: The study presents and causally tests a multi-stage detection–safety-neuron–refusal circuit, with component ablations, activation patching, and reinforcement. This refines the single-direction account, though it does not directly compare geometric models such as a cone or affine subspace.
record.gate_note: The study derives layer-specific refusal directions from harmful–neutral response differences and includes a comparison with activation steering. That comparison measures safety on adversarial harmful prompts, not over-refusal on harmless prompts, so it does not test the harmless-refusal part of V1. Appendix Table 11 measures detection-head and refusal-head signals across input types, but does not independently measure a harmfulness judgment and a refusal decision; it is not recorded as a V5 result row. Appendix Tables 2 and 4–5 and Tables 7–9 and 12–25 report further scaling, safety, and utility outcomes, but are not separately cataloged here where they duplicate the main circuit findings or do not measure a version-specific claim.
record.test_reason: The study builds a per-layer refusal direction (mean post-MLP residual on refusal responses minus helpful responses) and uses it as a yardstick. It scores attention heads and MLP neurons by how they write onto it, then scales those components to raise safety. It never ablates or adds one difference-in-means direction to test V1, never compares geometries (V4), and never dissociates a harmfulness representation from the refusal decision (V5). Its detection heads are also scored on the same refusal direction (Appendix D). Its circuit findings concern component-level pathways, a related but different construct, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. The main results report the study's own method (CBSE) against baselines.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors also claim the detection–refusal circuit recurs across six architectures. They report that circuit-guided weight scaling raises GCG safety by 26.5 points on average for a 1.7-point average benchmark accuracy drop. They note LLaMA3 as an outlier with a weak detection→refusal pathway.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives layer-specific refusal directions from paired harmful and neutral responses, identifies distinct attention heads and MLP neurons, and ablates or scales selected component weights. It does not project out one global difference-in-means direction at every layer and position. The main intervention strengthens multiple circuit components rather than removing a single direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The detection-to-refusal patching effect varies by architecture, with LLaMA3 substantially weaker than the other five models. The appendices also report sensitivity to component-selection ratios and scaling factors.

fits_no_version.finding: Activation patching of detection-head output shifts refusal-head contribution to the refusal direction in both directions in five of six models (forward 19.5–34.6%, backward 39.4–70.6%); LLaMA3 is negligible or weak (0.7% / 18.2%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Upstream attention heads that attend to harmful tokens causally feed downstream refusal heads; the strength of this pathway is model-dependent.

fits_no_version.finding: Zeroing top-attributed detection heads or safety neurons drops refusal-head contribution far more than random removal of the same number of components.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-head activity depends on specific upstream heads and MLP neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: Zeroing 1–5% of top-attributed circuit components collapses GCG safety rates (e.g. LLaMA3 75→2%, Mistral 51→0% at 5%), though LLaMA2 retains 16%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Knocking out a small set of refusal-aligned components removes most refusal under attack, with model-dependent completeness.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding the study's layer-wise refusal direction at inference raises GCG safety by a model-dependent amount (81→82, 45→70, 59→96).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time addition of a refusal direction partially restores refusal under GCG attacks, depending on the model.

record.problems: The main safety evaluations use an automated Llama-Guard classifier. The paper states that many reported safety rates come from a single generation run per configuration; a five-seed analysis is provided in Appendix A.2. The human evaluation uses one annotator on a pooled sample of 100 responses. The paper's LLaMA3 model naming is inconsistent: the setup lists LLaMA-38B-Instruct, while tables and text refer to LLaMA3.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix Table 11's detection-head/refusal-head signal measurements across five input types were omitted because they do not independently test harmfulness judgment versus refusal decision. The numerous additional attack, judge, parameter-sensitivity, and benchmark results in Appendix Tables 2 and 4–9 and 12–25 were not extracted where they repeat the main intervention findings or do not directly measure a claim version.

untested.parts: No ablation of a single difference-in-means direction across layers and positions. No addition on harmless prompts. Steering appears only as a GCG-safety comparator.
No abliteration-style edit; the weight edits amplify safety components.
No analysis of whether jailbreaks suppress the direction; no adversarial training against its ablation.
No comparison of single versus multi-direction, cone or affine geometry. All components are scored against one direction per layer.
No separate harmfulness representation decoded. Detection heads are scored on the refusal direction, and no dissociation between harm judgment and refusal is shown.
No transfer across languages, variants or base-to-instruct models.

record.verdict_notes: The refusal direction here comes from responses (mean over generated tokens of the harmful-prompt response minus the neutral-prompt response), per layer, from 51 probe pairs. It is not Arditi's prompt-token difference-in-means. The 'Activation-Steering (Arditi et al.)' baseline uses this direction. The ablations zero heads and neurons rather than projecting out a direction. Safety rates come from single runs; baseline numbers for the same configuration vary across tables (e.g. LLaMA3 GCG original: 72, 75, 77, 81, 84), consistent with the seed noise reported in Table 7. Over-refusal on OR-Bench rises after CBSE for five of six models (e.g. Mistral 31.6→48.3), which the authors call modest.

versions.untested_parts: The activation-steering comparison adds a layer-wise refusal direction but does not measure refusal on harmless prompts. The study does not ablate one difference-in-means direction from every layer and position, nor test whether such ablation preserves general abilities.
The weight edits reinforce components to improve safety; the study does not test an abliteration-style weight edit intended to remove refusal.
The study evaluates jailbreak attacks but does not test whether they work by suppressing a refusal direction, or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
The study tests a multi-component circuit and interactions among components, not whether refusal has a cone or affine geometry, or a dominant direction plus smaller directions.

The study distinguishes harmful-detection components from refusal components and patches between them, but does not independently decode or measure a harmfulness judgment separately from the refusal decision.
The study reports recurring circuit organization across model architectures, but does not test transfer of the same direction across languages, base and instruct models, or model variants.
The study does not vary how or when refusal training is done.
The study does not evaluate reasoning models that reason before answering.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Detection-head and safety-neuron interventions across the evaluated architectures
reader_labels.reason: Targeted ablation lowers refusal-head contribution while random removal has little effect, and circuit ablation substantially reduces GCG safety; the patching results also show contributions from an upstream detection component. Rows R3-R16 and R17-R28.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: LLaMA3 patching and model-specific ablation outcomes
reader_labels.reason: LLaMA3 has a negligible 0.7% forward patch effect and a weaker 18.2% backward effect; the ablation table also includes a Guanaco condition where safety rises from 3% to 9%. Rows R1-R2 and R20.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Replacing detection-head output changes downstream refusal-head contribution in both directions in five models, with a weaker pathway in LLaMA3, consistent with distinct detection and refusal stages. Rows R1-R12.
